title: Pulmonary Metastases from a Hemangiopericytoma/Solitary Fibrous Tumor Spectrum Neoplasm in a Patient with a Poorly Documented Thigh Tumor: A Case Report
journal: Reports - Clinical Practice and Surgical Cases
question: How can lung metastases from a poorly documented thigh hemangiopericytoma/solitary fibrous tumor be missed, and how was their origin found?

bottom_line.question: How can lung metastases from a poorly documented thigh hemangiopericytoma/solitary fibrous tumor be missed, and how was their origin found?
bottom_line.answer: A young woman with hemoptysis had two lung masses. They were metastases from a thigh tumor that had been assumed benign, and this was recognised only after the old thigh pathology report was retrieved. Despite both lung resections and chemotherapy, she died within 18 months.

provenance.quote: The patient died within 18 months of the initial pulmonary diagnosis.

sections.title: A Missing Thigh Tumor Record Delays a Lung Diagnosis
sections.markdown: A 33-year-old woman came to an emergency department in Romania coughing up blood. Scans showed a large mass in each lung. Her doctors considered lung tumors, a parasitic cyst and benign growths. The real cause came to light only after surgeons had removed both masses. She had twice had surgery for a thigh tumor, her records on it were poor, and that tumor had been malignant. The lung masses were metastases from it. The report shows how this gap in her history delayed the diagnosis.

sections.title: The Tumor: Solitary Fibrous Tumor, Once Called Hemangiopericytoma
sections.markdown:
**Solitary fibrous tumor (SFT)** is a rare connective tissue tumor that can arise almost anywhere in the body. Older pathology reports often called it hemangiopericytoma (HPC), after the way its cells cluster around blood vessels under the microscope. The current WHO classification places soft tissue tumors once labeled HPC in the SFT category. The authors use "HPC" only where the patient's old records did.

SFT is uncommon, with a reported incidence of 0.023 cases per 100,000 people, and it behaves in different ways. Many cases are cured by surgery. Others come back or spread, sometimes years later. Doctors judge the risk from the patient's age, the tumor's size, its mitotic activity (how fast its cells divide) and necrosis (areas of dead tumor tissue). Because relapse can come late, long follow-up is advised. Imaging can show how far the disease extends but cannot identify it. That takes tissue under a microscope. The stain that confirms SFT, called STAT6 immunohistochemistry, was not available in this retrospective case. So the authors describe the tumor cautiously as a "hemangiopericytoma/solitary fibrous tumor spectrum neoplasm."

sections.title: How the Case Unfolded: Workup, Surgery and the Missing Thigh Report
sections.markdown:
She did not smoke, had no workplace exposure to lung toxins and had no relevant medical history. Her father had had lung cancer. Bronchoscopy (a camera passed into the airways) found blood in both lungs and a clot blocking the airway to the left upper lobe. No biopsy was taken. There was no visible lesion inside the airways to sample, and because the tumor was thought to be full of blood vessels, a biopsy risked bleeding.

CT showed a solid mass up to 11 cm across in the left upper lobe, growing into the membrane that lines the central chest. A second mass, up to about 6 cm, sat in the right middle lobe and had grown into the outer lining of the lung. There was no sign of spread elsewhere. A blood test for hydatid disease (a tapeworm infection) was negative. Tuberculosis is common in Romania, so it was an early suspect, but the solid, well-defined masses pointed toward cancer.

Both masses looked removable, so she had two operations. The left upper lobe came out first, and the final pathology showed a malignant tumor in the HPC/SFT spectrum. Six cycles of cisplatin-based chemotherapy followed. Then surgeons removed the right middle lobe, which held the same tumor.

Because this tumor type is known to spread, the team went back over her history. She then told them about two thigh operations. The first, five years earlier, had reportedly been diagnosed as a "myoma," a benign muscle tumor. The second, two years earlier, treated a recurrence. The family never obtained that pathology report because they assumed the lump was benign. When the report was finally retrieved, it showed malignant hemangiopericytoma, and the lung masses were reinterpreted as metastases from the thigh.

sections.title: Outcome
sections.markdown: Within a year she had metastases in the front and back of the brain, new lesions in both lungs and the mediastinum (the central chest compartment), and one under the skin. Further treatment did not control the disease. She died within 18 months of the lung diagnosis.

sections.title: Lessons, Context and Limitations
sections.markdown:
The main lesson is about diagnosis. The thigh pathology report settled where the lung tumors came from. Without it, the list of possible causes stayed broad and the answer came late. The authors make three recommendations for patients who have unexplained masses in both lungs and a history of recurring soft tissue tumors:

- Retrieve earlier pathology reports, even for lumps that were called benign.
- Keep these patients under long-term surveillance.
- Don't expect imaging alone to settle the diagnosis.

For context, they cite a study of 213 patients with HPC of the brain. The most common sites of spread were bone (19.6%), pleura and lung (18.4%), liver (17.6%) and vertebrae (14.1%). HPC that starts in the lung is rarer still. In those cases, coughing blood and pain have been linked to worse outcomes, and growth into the airway (seen in about 10%) to better ones. The authors believe this is the first documented Romanian case of HPC spreading to the lung. One earlier Romanian report described a tumor that started in the lung.

There is little evidence on chemotherapy for advanced SFT, so treatment should be planned case by case by a team of specialists. In this case the regimen details were not recorded. No scan exists from between the chemotherapy and the second surgery, so it can't be known whether the drugs shrank the right-lung tumor.

The authors state the report's limits. It is retrospective. The records for the thigh tumor, the bronchoscopy and the operations are incomplete, so the surgical margins and lymph node status are unknown. The STAT6 result and full chemotherapy details are missing. Because the patient died, her own account could not be collected.

The main diagnostic challenge was the absence of complete documentation regarding the patient’s previous recurrent thigh tumor at the time of pulmonary presentation. sources.abstract: Background and Clinical Significance: Solitary fibrous tumor (SFT), historically termed hemangiopericytoma (HPC), is a rare fibroblastic mesenchymal neoplasm with variable biological behavior. Pulmonary involvement is uncommon and may represent either a primary thoracic tumor or metastatic disease from an extrapulmonary site. Its clinical course ranges from indolent, surgically curable disease to aggressive malignancy with local recurrence and distant dissemination. In this retrospective case, confirmatory STAT6 immunohistochemistry was unavailable; therefore, the tumor is described as a hemangiopericytoma/solitary fibrous tumor spectrum neoplasm. Case Presentation: We report the case of a 33-year-old woman who presented with sudden-onset hemoptysis and was found to have two large, well-defined bilateral pulmonary masses. Initial clinical and radiological evaluation raised suspicion of primary pulmonary tumors or other benign lesions. Because both lesions were considered resectable, staged pulmonary resections were performed. Subsequent reassessment of the patient’s medical history revealed previous surgeries for a poorly documented recurrent thigh tumor, later confirmed to represent the primary malignant hemangiopericytoma/solitary fibrous tumor spectrum neoplasm. Despite staged pulmonary resections, systemic chemotherapy, and further oncologic management, the disease progressed rapidly, with cerebral, bilateral pulmonary, mediastinal, and subcutaneous metastases. The patient died within 18 months of the initial pulmonary diagnosis. Conclusions: This case highlights the diagnostic difficulty of metastatic pulmonary hemangiopericytoma, particularly when the primary soft tissue tumor is inadequately documented. It emphasizes the importance of detailed clinical history, retrieval of previous histopathological reports, and long-term surveillance in patients with soft tissue tumors, even when initially considered benign.
sources.sec1-reports-09-00274/p1: Solitary fibrous tumor (SFT) is a rare fibroblastic mesenchymal neoplasm that may arise at virtually any anatomical site. The term “hemangiopericytoma” (HPC), initially used for tumors with a characteristic perivascular growth pattern, has historical significance; however, current classifications incorporate soft-tissue tumors previously designated as HPC within the SFT spectrum [,,]. In this report, the term HPC is retained only when referring to the historical terminology used in the available pathology records. SFT exhibits heterogeneous biological behavior. Although many tumors remain localized, local recurrence and distant metastasis, including delayed relapse, may occur. Risk assessment incorporates clinicopathological variables such as patient age, tumor size, mitotic activity, and necrosis; therefore, long-term surveillance is warranted [,,]. The rarity of this entity is reflected in population-based data, with a reported incidence of 0.023 per 100,000 []. Thoracic involvement is uncommon and may represent either a primary thoracic SFT or metastatic disease from an extrapulmonary primary. Malignant thoracic tumors may show local invasion and distant dissemination, emphasizing the importance of complete staging and prolonged follow-up []. Imaging is essential for assessing tumor extent and planning treatment but is not diagnostic; histopathological examination, supported by immunohistochemistry when tissue is available, remains central to diagnosis [,]. Complete surgical resection is the principal treatment when technically feasible. The management of locally advanced or metastatic disease should be individualized through multidisciplinary discussion because evidence supporting systemic treatment remains limited []. In patients presenting with unusual pulmonary masses and a history of recurrent soft-tissue tumors, active retrieval and review of prior pathology are essential to establish the origin of the pulmonary lesions.
